And so in order for a service road to be functional, you need to, at these end points, you need to separate it either by use of an interchange or you need a lot of land to spread those service roads out. And typically you wouldn't find that in urban setting. If you look at, for example, the intersection spacing in Hinton, you've got a 2000 meter intersection spacing between intersections, as well the right of way that you've got there is several hundred meters wide. In Red Deer, the spacing along Gasoline Alley between those intersections is almost 2,800 meters. In Beaumont, adjacent to L'Oreve, we're talking about a 1,600 meter distance. So what happens when you move those intersections, those service road intersections closer together, you end up with movements of vehicles going back and forth between lanes, getting on from one service road or off on the next one, it's called a weave. So you imagine these vehicles weaving in and out of each other to try to get onto the road from a service road or off of the road from a service road. So at 1,600 meters, you don't have enough space between your intersections to provide an adequate distance for those movements to take place. And so you end up again with a lot of conflict points within a very short space. Where Beaumont currently ends, where the urban area of Beaumont currently ends and the commercial area to the south, to the Edmonton city limits is only gonna be about 1,600 meters. And the Edmonton section of this road is going to be an arterial road. And the arterial road standards for the city of Edmonton, they typically you would see about 300 meter spacing between intersections along an arterial road. And so what's being proposed for the REV is a similar intersection spacing along there. And what it does is provides an adequate number of intersections for access to those commercial and residential areas. You're not loading up one intersection or two intersections with all that traffic, you're spreading it out. And by having those intersections at that 300 plus or minus meter spacing, what it allows is a progression of that traffic through those various lights. If you put all of that traffic onto a single intersection or onto two intersections, those side streets need more green time. They need more time when 50th street would be red and the side streets would be green to get all that traffic out onto 50th street. So by actually putting in more intersections and spacing them appropriately, you can get a much more efficient operation on 50th street. So while service roads may provide a solution in some situations, given this is a very tight urban context and in the long run, it's gonna be a very urban area and not a lot of land and you don't have really long intersection spacing, it's likely not the best solution in terms of achieving flows. I think the perception is that a service road solves problems, but what a service road does is concentrates a lot of activity in a very small space, creates conflicts, and it leads to operational challenges that aren't easily resolved.
